In summary, our research is concerned with
the estimation of the elasticities of substitution in the production of agricultural output.
the effects of input substitution on the use of agricultural inputs, particularly fertilizers and pesticides.
the estimation of aggregate U.S. demands for fertilizer, pesticides, and other inputs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of input price changes on input use vary widely across the agricultural sector.
the elasticity of substitution between fertilizer and pesticides is small, but the elasticity of substitution within each input group is large.
the results are sensitive to assumptions and that further analysis is needed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pesticide use is much more sensitive to price changes than fertilizer use.
a 100 percent pesticide tax would reduce pesticide use by about 17 percent, and that a 10-percent fertilizer charge would reduce fertilizer use by about 1 percent.
the results of this research are not surprising but do confirm that the CGE model assumptions are not unreasonable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of input charges are very sensitive to the way the model is set up.
the effects of a pesticide charge are much more pronounced than those of a fertilizer charge.
the elasticity of substitution among inputs is a crucial determinant of how effective an environmental policy will be in reducing use of a specific input.
